stem:
The curve $C$ has equation $y = \mathrm{f}(x)$, where
$$\mathrm{f}(x) = \frac{(3x - 2)^2}{x\sqrt{x}}, \qquad x > 0.$$

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that $\mathrm{f}(x)$ can be written as $9x^{\frac{1}{2}} - 12x^{-\frac{1}{2}} + 4x^{-\frac{3}{2}}$. (3)

mark_scheme.for: Squares out the bracket to get a 3-term quadratic and writes the denominator $x\sqrt{x}$ as $x^{\frac{3}{2}}$ (or divides each term by $x\sqrt{x}$ with some correct index work)
mark_scheme.notes: Accept a slip in the numerator, e.g. a wrong middle coefficient, as long as there are 3 terms and the denominator becomes a single power of $x$

mark_scheme.for: Correct numerator $9x^2 - 12x + 4$ over $x^{\frac{3}{2}}$, or at least two of the three terms correctly divided
Reaches $9x^{\frac{1}{2}} - 12x^{-\frac{1}{2}} + 4x^{-\frac{3}{2}}$ with every index step shown and no errors
mark_scheme.notes: cso; the division of each term must be shown, not just the final printed line

hints: Start by expanding $(3x-2)^2$, then write $x\sqrt{x}$ as a single power of $x$.
Divide each term of the numerator separately, subtracting indices.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Using your answer to part (a), find $\mathrm{f}'(x)$. Then find the exact gradient of $C$ at the point on $C$ with $x = 4$. (3)

mark_scheme.for: Differentiates the three-term power form from (a), with at least one power of $x$ lowered by 1 and multiplied by its old index

mark_scheme.notes: oe, any correct unsimplified form; isw

solution.working: $\mathrm{f}(x) = 9x^{\frac{1}{2}} - 12x^{-\frac{1}{2}} + 4x^{-\frac{3}{2}}$, so differentiate term by term using $\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}(x^n) = nx^{n-1}$

hints: Use the form from part (a) instead of the original fraction: each term is now a power of $x$.
Be careful with negative indices: lowering $-\frac{1}{2}$ by 1 gives $-\frac{3}{2}$.

pitfalls.text: A common slip is to write $x\sqrt{x}$ as $x^{\frac{1}{2}}$. Indices add when you multiply, so $x \times x^{\frac{1}{2}} = x^{\frac{3}{2}}$. With the wrong power, none of your terms match the printed form and you lose the M1.

Students often write $\frac{4}{x^{\frac{3}{2}}}$ as $4x^{\frac{3}{2}}$. A power in the denominator moves up with a negative index, so it is $4x^{-\frac{3}{2}}$. If you drop the sign you can't get the A1*.
Don't try to simplify by cancelling $\sqrt{x}$ against only part of $(3x-2)^2$. Expand fully first, then divide every term by the same $x^{\frac{3}{2}}$, or you lose the M1.

When you differentiate $-12x^{-\frac{1}{2}}$, the new power is $-\frac{3}{2}$ (not $\frac{1}{2}$), and $-12 \times -\frac{1}{2} = +6$. If either the sign or the index is wrong, you lose the first A1 and then the value $\frac{45}{16}$.
If you try to differentiate $\frac{(3x-2)^2}{x\sqrt{x}}$ by differentiating the top and bottom separately, the method is invalid and you lose the M1. Use the power form from part (a).
